```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", dpi = 96, out.width = "80%")
```

This tutorial runs SigDoTS on the simulated dataset that comes with the package and shows
how to read every part of the result. It takes about half a minute to run.


```{r setup}
library(SigDoTS)
```

## The example data

`sigdots_example` has 900 spots on a 30 x 30 grid and 200 genes. The spots belong to three
true domains of 300 spots each. Forty of the genes ("marker" genes) have different means in
the three domains; the noise is correlated between nearby spots and between genes.

```{r data}
str(sigdots_example, max.level = 1)
sigdots_example$x[1:3, c(1:3, 198:200)]
table(sigdots_example$region)
```

SigDoTS needs two things: the expression matrix `x` (one row per spot, one column per gene,
already normalised) and the coordinates `coords` (one row per spot, two columns, in the same
order). The true regions are not used; we keep them to compare with the result.

If your data are in a Seurat or SpatialExperiment object, pass the object itself instead of the
two matrices; see `vignette("own-data")`.

## Running SigDoTS

The one choice to make is the number of candidate domains, `K0`. SigDoTS first divides the
spots into `K0` candidate domains (by default with k-means on the first 15 principal components). `K0`
should be larger than the number of domains you expect, so that each candidate domain lies
inside one true domain; SigDoTS then decides which candidate domains to merge. Here we use `K0 = 5` for
three true domains.

```{r run}
fit <- sigdots(sigdots_example$x, sigdots_example$coords, K0 = 5)
```

While it runs, SigDoTS prints one line per test: where in the tree the test is, how many
spots and candidate domains that part has, the decision, the number of simulated datasets it
used and the time it took. `verbose = FALSE` silences these lines.

## The split tree

```{r print}
fit
```

How to read the tree:

* Each line starting with a number in brackets is a part of the tree (a *node*), with its
  number of spots and the candidate domains it contains.
* `split` or `no split` is the decision of the test at that node. SigDoTS tests from the
  top: the whole sample first; the two sides of a split are tested in turn.
* `=> DOMAIN k` marks a part that was not split further: it is the k-th final domain.
  Inside a domain, only the candidate domains and their sizes are listed.
* A single candidate domain (here candidate domain 4, `[4]`) is never tested; when its parent is split,
  it becomes a domain by itself.

## The tests

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

The table has one row per test: `statistic` is the split statistic of the data (between 0
and 1; smaller means a clearer split), `null_used` the number of simulated single-domain
datasets the test used, `p` the p-value, `level` the significance level of this test, and
`decision` the outcome. A split is made when `p <= level`. The level of a test on m of the
n spots is `alpha * (m - 1) / (n - 1)` (here `alpha = 0.05` and n = 900), which keeps the
probability of any false split in the whole tree at most `alpha`. Every column is explained
in `?summary.sigdots`.

By default each test simulates 10 datasets, raised for a test to the smallest number with
which the p-value can reach the level (19 at the first test), and stops as soon as the
decision cannot change. With so few datasets a p-value takes only a few values; the decision
is what the test establishes. Finer p-values cost more time (`B_min`, `B_max`).

The table is also returned as a data frame:

```{r summary-table}
summary(fit)$tests
```

## Getting the domains

```{r domains}
head(domains(fit))
table(domain = domains(fit)$domain, true_region = sigdots_example$region)
```

The three domains are the three true regions. `domains(fit)` has one row per spot in the
order of the data, so it can be joined to any other per-spot information. If the data came
from a Seurat or SpatialExperiment object, `add_domains(object, fit)` writes the domain of
every spot into the object.

## Plots

`plot()` draws four kinds of plots, all ggplot2 objects that you can modify as usual.

The final domains, with the domain numbers and the boundaries between domains:

```{r plot-domains, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit)
```

The candidate domains, with the boundaries of the final domains, showing which candidate domains
were merged:

```{r plot-candidates, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit, type = "candidates")
```

The split tree, with each test's decision, p-value and level:

```{r plot-tree, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "95%"}
plot(fit, type = "tree")
```

The spatial correlation of the noise, as SigDoTS estimated it at the first test for the
single-domain model: the points are the correlation between pairs of spots at each distance
(in units of the distance between neighbouring spots), after removing each candidate domain's
mean and averaged over genes; the line is what the fitted model gives. `eta` is the share of
the noise variance that is spatially correlated and `ell` how far the correlation reaches;
here both are close to the values the data were simulated with (0.5 and 3). The line following
the points means the model describes the spatial correlation of the data. `test = ` draws
the same plot for another test of the tree.

```{r plot-correlogram, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2}
plot(fit, type = "correlogram")
```

## Reproducibility

The same data, arguments and `seed` (default 1) give the same result, whatever the number
of cores (`n_cores`). SigDoTS does not change the random-number state of your session.

## When a part of the tree cannot be tested

To estimate `eta` and `ell`, SigDoTS needs enough pairs of spots from the same candidate domain
at several distances: at least 4 distance bins with at least 200 such pairs each. A part
of the tree with very few spots (on a regular grid, fewer than about 80) does not have
them. SigDoTS then leaves that part untested, still tests the rest of the tree, warns at
the end, marks the part `[!] NOT TESTED` in the tree, and gives its spots no domain
(`NA` in `domains()`). Using fewer candidate domains (a smaller `K0`) makes the parts larger.
